newsitem.title: GERMANY: German DAX surges through 2,700, rally to continue.
newsitem.headline: German DAX surges through 2,700, rally to continue.

text.p: German shares surged through the psychological level of 2,700 late on Friday boosted by weaker-than-expected U.S. jobs data, which put a dampener on expectations of imminent U.S. interest rate hikes.
The DAX index of 30 blue chip shares closed floor trade up 6.78 points, or 0.25 percent, at 2,683.28, overtaking a high of 2680.10 touched during Wednesday's close.
After the U.S. data the IBIS DAX index of electronic trade went on to make further gains, closing at an all-time high of 2,704.25, gaining 18.96 points or 0.71 percent.
U.S. September non-farm payrolls came in down 40,000, confounding market expectations of a rise of 166,000.
Dealers said the German market had seen quite a lot of interest from American investors, adding that some dealers were even starting to talk about the DAX reaching the magical 3,000 point level.
"That we've reached a new high before a holiday and then we've gone further before the weekend is of course a very bullish sign," said one dealer.

Earlier on, stocks were supported by a strong dollar against the mark, which helped export-oriented German stocks. Later in the day the dollar sank back and the IBIS DAX index looked instead to Wall Street for inspiration.
Volumes were light after many market players took a long weekend, following the Germany Unity Day holiday on Thursday. "Most people closed their books for the week on Wednesday," said one trader.

Dealers said the interim report of Allianz AG Holding on Monday would attract a lot of interest. Next Friday U.S. figures will be in the spotlight once more when September producer prices and retail sales data is released.

Building group Holzmann AG was Friday's loss leader, tumbling 18 marks, over five percent, to 332 marks, after a Bild newspaper report said that its chief executive could be sacked and replaced by the head of diversified industrial group Metallgesellschaft AG.
MG denied the report as nonsense and Holzmann called the article "factually incorrect and speculative." Holzmann on Wednesday denied reports that the group had liquidity problems.
Airline company Lufthansa gained ground, with traders saying the firm was cutting three South American routes due to lack of demand.
